claims.evidence: Macmillan: small sample of bone marrow taken from the back of the hip bone (pelvis) or occasionally the breastbone; NHS leaflets: done to find the cause of abnormal blood counts.
Macmillan: small sample from the back of the hip bone. 'Spongy tissue' not shown in the retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: A bone marrow biopsy takes a small sample of bone marrow, usually from the back of the hip bone.

claims.evidence: NHS leaflet: sample checked under a microscope for abnormal cells; used to find the cause of abnormal blood counts. 'Cancerous' not stated directly.
claims.newSentence: It is done to find out why blood counts are abnormal and to look for abnormal cells in the marrow.

claims.evidence: Macmillan: local anaesthetic used, sedative may be offered, may ache or feel bruised for a few days.
Leaflets give aspirate results in about 2 days, 1 to 2 weeks for fuller results, up to four weeks; results usually given at the next clinic appointment.
claims.newSentence: Results can take from a few days up to about four weeks, depending on the hospital and the tests, and are usually discussed at a clinic appointment.

claims.evidence: Plain textbook definition; not quoted in retrieved text.
Macmillan: a small sample of bone marrow is taken; NHS leaflets: checked under a microscope.
Macmillan: taken from the back of the hip bone (pelvis) or occasionally the breastbone (sternum). 'Only rarely' reworded.
claims.newSentence: Macmillan says the sample is taken from the back of the hip bone, which is part of the pelvis, or occasionally from the breastbone.

claims.evidence: Macmillan describes an aspirate and a trephine, often done together at the same site.
Macmillan: aspirate is liquid marrow drawn into a syringe; trephine is a small solid core taken with a slightly larger needle.
NHS leaflets: to find the cause of abnormal blood counts and check marrow cells for abnormalities; 'cancerous' not stated directly.
claims.newSentence: The test is usually done to work out why blood counts are abnormal and to look for abnormal cells.

claims.evidence: Leaflet summary: low or high red cells, white cells or platelets, and infection among reasons. Exact wording of 'low red cells' not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: NHS leaflets list a low or high number of red cells, white cells or platelets, and infection, among the reasons.

claims.evidence: NHS leaflets: a marrow test can give information a blood test cannot, and marrow involvement may affect treatment.
Rotherham leaflet: local anaesthetic always used, Entonox (gas and air) also available. 'Or' is wrong; gas and air is an addition.
claims.newSentence: Local anaesthetic is used to numb the area, and gas and air may also be available.

claims.evidence: Macmillan: a sedative may be offered. 'Can be requested' not shown.
claims.newSentence: Medicine to help the person relax, called a sedative, may be offered.

claims.evidence: Body position not found in retrieved text.
Macmillan: may feel uncomfortable for a few seconds when the liquid marrow is withdrawn into the syringe.
The 20 to 30 minutes comes from Macmillan's non-Hodgkin lymphoma booklet, not the biopsy page; 'biopsy takes only a few minutes' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A Macmillan booklet says the test takes about 20 to 30 minutes, though hospitals vary.

claims.evidence: A hospital leaflet says the whole appointment takes about an hour including discussion beforehand.
claims.newSentence: One hospital leaflet says the whole appointment takes about an hour.

claims.evidence: Rotherham leaflet: dressings are applied and kept dry for a set time; times vary between hospitals.
claims.newSentence: A dressing is placed over the area, and hospital leaflets say how long to keep it on and dry.

claims.evidence: Macmillan: if sedation is used, advises not driving for 24 hours, having someone take you home and someone stay overnight.
claims.newSentence: After sedation, Macmillan advises not driving for 24 hours and having someone take the person home and stay with them overnight.

claims.evidence: Macmillan and leaflets: may ache or feel bruised for a few days.

Leaflet search summary: patients are usually asked about blood thinners beforehand; one leaflet says NSAIDs can worsen bleeding. A second search found nothing specific, so only the 'asked beforehand' part is kept.
claims.newSentence: Hospital leaflets say patients are usually asked about blood-thinning medicines beforehand.

claims.evidence: NTH leaflet: contact the Haematology Day Unit about swelling or redness; UCLH lists GP, NHS 111 or A&E if severe.
claims.newSentence: Leaflets say to contact the hospital team about swelling or redness at the site; a GP or NHS 111 can also advise.

claims.evidence: NHS leaflet: aching may last a few days, bruising expected and settles in a few days. 'One to four days' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Soreness and bruising at the site are common and usually last a few days.

claims.evidence: Leaflets: complications are uncommon; serious events rare.
Leaflet: some bleeding at the needle site usually stops when pressure is applied, leaving a small bruise. 'End of procedure' not stated.
claims.newSentence: Bleeding at the site usually stops with pressure, sometimes leaving a small bruise.

claims.evidence: No retrieved text about low platelets and bleeding risk; the sentence may mislead.
Leaflets: infection rare; nerve injury rare; allergic reaction to the local anaesthetic possible.
claims.newSentence: Infection and nerve injury are described as rare, and an allergic reaction to the numbing medicine is listed as a possible risk.

claims.evidence: Leaflets give different timings for results.
Royal Marsden: up to two weeks; Whittington: up to four weeks; Milton Keynes: appointment 3 to 4 weeks after.
Gloucestershire: usually you will be given the results at your next clinic appointment.
claims.newSentence: Results are usually given at the next clinic appointment.
